cases.checks: Of 1 published vulnerability in Tencent/WeKnora@a20541cd, how many does a scan capped at $3 report?

detail.what: GHSA-78H3-63C4-5FQC (injection) WeKnora MCP stdio 配置命令注入 (CVE-2026-22688) - client.go

findings.title: Any authenticated user can list all tenants and harvest every API key
findings.description:
Entry: internal/router/router.go:298 (tenantRoutes.GET("", handler.ListTenants)) -> internal/handler/tenant.go:251
Attacker: any authenticated user, including one who just self-registered through the public POST /api/v1/auth/register, crossing the tenant isolation boundary and reading every other tenant's record.
The handler takes no input and performs no check at all: it calls h.service.ListTenants(ctx) (internal/handler/tenant.go:251), which is internal/application/service/tenant.go:101-110, which calls s.repo.ListTenants(ctx), whose query is an unfiltered r.db.WithContext(ctx).Order("created_at DESC").Find(&tenants) (internal/application/repository/tenant.go:47-53). Nothing on the path filters by the caller's tenant and nothing compares against the tenant id that the middleware stored in the context (internal/middleware/auth.go:131). The response at lines 264-269 serializes []*types.Tenant directly, and types.Tenant.APIKey is serialized as "api_key" (internal/types/tenant.go:61) with no json:"-".
The two sibling routes that do expose cross-tenant data, /tenants/all and /tenants/search, both require cfg.Tenant.EnableCrossTenantAccess AND user.CanAccessAllTenants (internal/handler/tenant.go:294-305 and 354-365); GET /tenants has no such guard, even though its own doc comment claims it returns "the tenants the current user can access" (line 240).
Impact: one request returns every tenant in the system together with its API key, and that API key is a first-class credential accepted by the middleware's X-API-Key door (internal/middleware/auth.go:149-191, which loads the tenant and compares t.APIKey to the presented value). The attacker can therefore enumerate tenants (sequential uint64 primary key), harvest all API keys, and then read and modify every tenant's knowledge bases, knowledge, chunks, sessions, messages and models. The admin-only /tenants/all endpoint is effectively bypassed.
Fix: gate GET /tenants on the same checks as /tenants/all (config flag plus user.CanAccessAllTenants) and make the default path return only the caller's own tenant; never serialize APIKey in tenant responses (json:"-" on the field and return a redacted DTO).

findings.title: Any authenticated user can overwrite another tenant's API key via PUT /tenants/:id
findings.description:
Entry: internal/router/router.go:296 (tenantRoutes.PUT("/:id", handler.UpdateTenant)) -> internal/handler/tenant.go:152-169
Attacker: any authenticated user, crossing the tenant boundary by writing to another tenant's record, with mass assignment over the request body.
The handler takes the id from the path (line 152), binds the entire request body into a types.Tenant with c.ShouldBindJSON(&tenantData) (line 160), overwrites the id with the path value (line 168) and calls h.service.UpdateTenant(ctx, &tenantData) (line 169). No check compares the path id with the caller's tenant id, and no field is whitelisted, so the attacker controls Name, Description, Status, StorageQuota, AgentConfig, WebSearchConfig and APIKey. The service then writes it with internal/application/repository/tenant.go:96: r.db.WithContext(ctx).Model(&types.Tenant{}).Where("id = ?", tenant.ID).Updates(tenant) — GORM's Updates with a struct writes every non-zero field, including api_key.
Nothing stops this: the only tenant-level authorization in the codebase is the CanAccessAllTenants check on /tenants/all and /tenants/search, neither of which runs here.
Impact: an attacker can set a victim tenant's api_key to a value they choose (e.g. by first creating their own tenant and copying its key format, or simply sending any non-empty string, which the repository stores as-is) and then authenticate as that tenant through the X-API-Key door in the middleware, taking over the tenant completely; alternatively, sending an empty api_key regenerates the victim's key and locks the victim's integrations out, and the same call can rewrite the tenant's global Agent/WebSearch/Conversation configuration and storage quota.
Fix: ignore any api_key/id/status field supplied by the client, load the tenant to update from the authentication context, and require the CanAccessAllTenants privilege (plus the config flag) before allowing any other tenant id.

findings.title: Any authenticated user can delete another tenant by guessing its ID
findings.description:
Entry: internal/router/router.go:297 (tenantRoutes.DELETE("/:id", handler.DeleteTenant)) -> internal/handler/tenant.go:210-219
Attacker: any authenticated user, crossing the tenant boundary to destroy another tenant's data.
The handler parses the tenant id from the path (line 210) and calls h.service.DeleteTenant(ctx, id) (line 219) -> internal/application/service/tenant.go:142-177 -> internal/application/repository/tenant.go:100-102, r.db.WithContext(ctx).Where("id = ?", id).Delete(&types.Tenant{}). The only validation is that the id is non-zero (service line 145). The caller's own tenant id, available in the context from the middleware, is never compared to the target id, and the CanAccessAllTenants privilege that guards /tenants/all and /tenants/search is not required.
Impact: any user can delete any other tenant by guessing its sequential id, wiping that organization's workspace record; there is no confirmation, no ownership check and no privileged role requirement on this route.
Fix: delete only the tenant bound to the authenticated caller (or require the cross-tenant privilege plus the config flag and an explicit confirmation token), and re-verify the caller's tenant id against the target id inside the service before the repository call.

findings.title: Deactivated users keep full API access until their access token expires
findings.description:
Entry: internal/middleware/auth.go:82 (userService.ValidateToken is the single gate for every protected route)
Attacker: a user whose account has been disabled by the operator (users.is_active = false), crossing the boundary the application itself draws when it refuses that account at the login door.
The middleware authenticates every /api/v1 request through userService.ValidateToken (internal/application/service/user.go:325-353). That function verifies the JWT signature, the signing method, the user_id claim and the revoked flag of the token row (lines 347-351), then returns s.userRepo.GetUserByID(ctx, userID) at line 353 without ever reading or checking user.IsActive. The IsActive check exists only in Login (internal/application/service/user.go:150-157), which returns "Account is disabled"; the user row carries the flag (internal/types/user.go:24) and the frontend only sees it as data. The repository lookup (internal/application/repository/user.go:34-43) filters soft-deleted rows only, so a deactivated-but-not-deleted user is returned as a valid principal and the middleware proceeds to set tenant context and call c.Next().
So disabling an account stops new password logins but does nothing to the token the user already holds: every protected route keeps working for the remaining 24 hours of the access token, and no token is revoked anywhere (RevokeTokensByUserID exists in internal/application/repository/user.go:149-152 but is never called from any handler or service; ChangePassword likewise never revokes existing sessions).
Impact: an account that the operator believes is cut off — a departed employee, a compromised account, a banned user — retains full access to its tenant's knowledge bases, documents, chat history and models until the access token expires, with no server-side way to end it short of deleting the user row.
Fix: check user.IsActive (and any other account-state flag) in ValidateToken before returning the user, and revoke the user's tokens on deactivation, password change and explicit removal via RevokeTokensByUserID.

findings.title: Disabled users can refresh tokens forever and keep account access
findings.description:
Entry: internal/router/router.go:337 (POST /api/v1/auth/refresh, whitelisted in internal/middleware/auth.go:23) -> internal/handler/auth.go:228
Attacker: a disabled user who still holds a refresh token, crossing the account-disable boundary and extending their access indefinitely without a password.
RefreshToken parses the refresh JWT (lines 361-370), checks the type claim is "refresh" (377-380), reads user_id (382-385), checks the token row is not revoked (387-391), loads the user at line 394 and, without inspecting user.IsActive, revokes the old refresh token and calls GenerateTokens at line 404, which issues a fresh 24h access token and a fresh 7-day refresh token (lines 267-322) and stores both in the token table. The endpoint is public by design, so no other middleware check runs before it.
Nothing on this path consults the account state: the only IsActive check in the whole codebase is in Login (internal/application/service/user.go:150-157). Because each refresh mints a new refresh token, a disabled user can keep the chain alive forever by refreshing within the 7-day window, and the newly issued access token then passes ValidateToken (which also ignores IsActive).
Impact: account deactivation is not enforced against the refresh door, so a removed or compromised user retains permanent, self-renewing access to the tenant's data even after the operator disables the account.
Fix: load the user before issuing tokens and reject refresh when user.IsActive is false (or when the user is soft-deleted), and revoke all of the user's tokens on deactivation so an existing refresh token cannot be redeemed.

findings.title: Any API key holder can revoke another user's session token via /auth/logout
findings.description:
Entry: internal/router/router.go:339 (POST /api/v1/auth/logout) -> internal/handler/auth.go:186
Attacker: a caller authenticated with a tenant API key, crossing the user boundary by revoking a token that belongs to a different user.
Logout reads the Authorization header (line 166), splits out the token string (lines 175-183) and passes it to h.userService.RevokeToken(ctx, token) (line 186) without ever checking that the token belongs to the authenticated caller. RevokeToken (internal/application/service/user.go:408-418) looks the token up by value alone (s.tokenRepo.GetTokenByValue -> internal/application/repository/user.go:114-123, Where("token = ?", tokenValue), no user_id predicate) and flips is_revoked to true. The handler never compares tokenRecord.UserID with the authenticated user, and the API-key branch of the middleware authenticates the request with a tenant key while deliberately not setting any user in the context (internal/middleware/auth.go:148-191), so the handler has no caller identity to compare against and performs no comparison. Critically, the middleware only uses the Bearer token when ValidateToken succeeds (internal/middleware/auth.go:80-145); a Bearer token that fails validation falls through to the X-API-Key branch, so a request carrying X-API-Key: <attacker's own key> plus Authorization: Bearer <victim's token string> is accepted and reaches this handler, which then revokes the victim's token.
Impact: anyone who obtains a user's token string (from a log, a shared URL, a screenshot, a browser extension, or a leaked client) and holds any valid API key can invalidate that user's session at will — a targeted denial of service and a way to force a victim off the platform — even though the token is not theirs.
Fix: resolve the caller from the context (the user set by the middleware) and revoke only tokens whose UserID matches the caller; treat API-key authenticated requests as having no user and reject /auth/logout for them, and never accept a token to revoke from a header that was not the credential used to authenticate the request.

findings.title: Tenant filter bypass via unescaped SQL alias in database_query tool
findings.description:
Entry: internal/agent/tools/database_query.go:202 (Execute reads args["sql"], which is produced by the agent's tool call from the chat user's request; the tool is registered for chat sessions in internal/application/service/agent_service.go:254-255).
Attacker: an authenticated tenant user who talks to the agent, crossing the tenant isolation boundary that the database_query tool explicitly promises ("All queries are automatically filtered by the logged-in user's tenant_id").
Path: user message -> agent LLM emits database_query tool call -> DatabaseQueryTool.Execute (line 198) -> validateAndSecureSQL (line 216) -> SQLSecurityValidator.ValidateAndSecure -> validateSelectStmt -> validateFromItem, which takes rv.Alias.Aliasname (line 492-494) and only lowercases it -> injectTenantConditions (line 744) interpolates that alias raw with fmt.Sprintf("%s.tenant_id = %d", alias, v.tenantID) at line 761 and splices the result into the statement at lines 776/782/786 -> the final string is executed as raw SQL via t.db.WithContext(ctx).Raw(securedSQL).Rows() at line 231.
Why nothing stops it: validateInput only rejects null bytes and checks length; pg_query parsing, the single-SELECT check, the table/function whitelist, the subquery/UNION/CTE bans, and the deparse step all operate on the AST, but the alias string is carried over from the AST and re-inserted as raw text after deparse. No character or identifier validation is applied to the alias, and the regex-based WHERE splicing in injectTenantConditions also treats the deparsed SQL as plain text. For example, the tool call sql = `SELECT id FROM knowledge_bases AS "true or true --"` passes every check; deparse emits SELECT id FROM knowledge_bases AS "true or true --", and injectTenantConditions produces `SELECT id FROM knowledge_bases AS "true or true --" WHERE true or true --.tenant_id = 5`, where the -- comments out the tenant predicate and the tautology makes the WHERE always true.
Impact: the automatic tenant_id filter is defeated, so the query returns rows for every tenant (knowledge_bases, knowledges, chunks, sessions, tenants), letting one tenant read another tenant's data and metadata through the agent's database_query tool, and any future use of this tool inherits the same bypass.
Fix: do not rebuild the SQL from raw alias text. Either re-deparse the AST after adding the tenant predicate (e.g., inject the predicate as an AST node and call pg_query.Deparse again), or quote the alias with pg_query/identifier quoting and validate it against a strict identifier pattern (letters, digits, underscore, max length) before interpolation; additionally, refuse aliases that are not plain identifiers and avoid regex-based WHERE splicing on deparsed text.

findings.title: Unbounded response buffering in tracing middleware can OOM the server
findings.description:
Entry: every authenticated route registered in internal/router/router.go:92-110, because middleware.TracingMiddleware() is installed at internal/router/router.go:89 and middleware.Logger() at line 68 for the whole /api/v1 group.
Attacker: any authenticated caller (self-registration is open at internal/middleware/auth.go:19-24), including an anonymous one for the small auth responses; the memory held is driven by the response size the server produces, not by the size of the request.
Path: middleware/trace.go:82-87 replaces c.Writer with responseBodyWriter whose Write appends every byte to a bytes.Buffer (lines 23-26), the handler writes its response through it, and line 97-100 then does `responseContent := responseBody.String()` and `span.SetAttributes(attribute.String("http.response.body", responseContent))`, copying the entire body again into an OTel span attribute; middleware/logger.go:146-151 installs a second identical unbounded buffer for the same request and reads it at lines 185-190.
Why nothing stops it: both buffers have no size limit — the only cap in logger.go is maxBodySize=10KB applied to the truncated *log copy* at lines 84-95, while the buffer itself (and the span attribute) keeps the whole body. Nothing on the path bounds response size: handlers such as DownloadKnowledgeFile (internal/handler/knowledge.go:515 `io.Copy(w, file)`) stream arbitrarily large stored files, and the unbounded search/message endpoints above produce arbitrarily large JSON, all of which pass through these buffers before reaching the client.
Impact: a single small GET can make the server hold the full response body in RAM (three copies counting the JSON encoding, the logger buffer and the span attribute) for the whole request duration; concurrent large downloads or large searches multiply this and can OOM the process, killing the API for every tenant.
Fix: wrap the response writer with a bounded capture (e.g. keep only the first N KB for logging/tracing and discard the rest), stop attaching the full response body to span attributes, and cap the streaming download endpoints so the response size is bounded independently of stored data.

findings.title: Any authenticated user can read any tenant's profile and API key by ID
findings.description:
Entry: internal/router/router.go:295 (GET /api/v1/tenants/:id) -> internal/handler/tenant.go:106.
Attacker: any self-registered authenticated user (registration is open at POST /api/v1/auth/register), crossing tenant isolation.
Path: the path parameter id is parsed at tenant.go:109 and passed straight to h.service.GetTenantByID(ctx, id) at line 116; the service (internal/application/service/tenant.go:83) and repository (internal/application/repository/tenant.go:35) load the row by primary key with no tenant or owner predicate, and the handler returns the whole tenant object at lines 129-132. The Tenant struct serializes api_key (internal/types/tenant.go:61), so the response contains the victim tenant's API key.
Why nothing stops it: the global Auth middleware (internal/middleware/auth.go:65) only proves that some valid JWT or API key was presented; it never compares the requested tenant id with the caller's tenant id. The sibling handlers ListAllTenants and SearchTenants do enforce user.CanAccessAllTenants (internal/handler/tenant.go:301 and 361), and the service even has an unused GetTenantByIDForUser (internal/application/service/tenant.go:317), so the ownership check is simply absent on this route.
Impact: any registered user can enumerate tenant ids, read every other tenant's profile and API key, and then use that key as X-API-Key (accepted at internal/middleware/auth.go:149-178) to fully act as the victim tenant - reading, modifying and deleting its knowledge bases, sessions, models and documents.
Fix: read the caller's tenant id from the auth context and reject the request when it does not equal the path id unless the caller has CanAccessAllTenants and cross-tenant access is enabled; never serialize api_key to non-owner callers.

findings.title: Stolen refresh token survives logout, letting attacker mint access tokens
findings.description:
Entry: internal/handler/auth.go:160 (POST /api/v1/auth/logout, calls RevokeToken at line 186).
Attacker: anyone holding the user's refresh token (stolen from client storage), crossing the session-termination boundary the logout endpoint is supposed to enforce.
Path: Logout passes only the Authorization access token to RevokeToken, which looks up that single row by value and marks it revoked (lines 408-417); the refresh token row created in GenerateTokens (lines 308-319) is never touched. POST /api/v1/auth/refresh is explicitly unauthenticated (internal/middleware/auth.go:23), and RefreshToken (lines 357-405) accepts the still-valid refresh token and returns a new access token plus a new refresh token.
Why nothing stops it: no code path revokes the refresh token on logout, and ChangePassword (internal/application/service/user.go:228-250) revokes nothing either; the repository even provides RevokeTokensByUserID (internal/application/repository/user.go:150) but it is never called.
Impact: logout and password change do not terminate the session; a stolen refresh token keeps minting access tokens for up to 7 days (renewable indefinitely) after the victim believes they have logged out, so account remediation cannot cut off the attacker.
Fix: on logout revoke the refresh token (and ideally all tokens for the session/user) and on password change revoke every outstanding token for that user.

findings.title: Unauthenticated user enumeration via distinct registration error messages
findings.description:
Entry: internal/router/router.go:335 (POST /api/v1/auth/register -> handler.Register, internal/handler/auth.go:51); the route is in the unauthenticated allow-list (internal/middleware/auth.go:21).
Attacker: an unauthenticated outsider with no account, crossing the boundary that should keep account membership private.
Path: the body is bound to types.RegisterRequest, then internal/application/service/user.go:77-85 returns distinct errors - 'user with this email already exists' and 'user with this username already exists' - which the handler wraps at line 80 in errors.NewBadRequestError("Registration failed").WithDetails(err.Error()).
Why nothing stops it: WithDetails stores the raw service error, and the global ErrorHandler middleware (internal/middleware/error_handler.go:23-33) copies appErr.Details into the JSON response as error.details, so the distinguishing text reaches the caller; login deliberately returns only 'Invalid email or password', so registration is the only oracle and nothing rate-limits or genericizes it.
Impact: an anonymous caller can confirm whether a given e-mail address or username has an account (and thus a workspace) on this deployment, which is exactly the account/personal-data disclosure the login flow avoids, and it feeds credential-stuffing and phishing against known addresses.
Fix: return one generic message ('registration failed' / 'email or username unavailable') and keep the specific reason only in the server log.

findings.title: Password change leaves existing tokens valid, so a stolen token keeps access
findings.description: Entry: internal/handler/auth.go:325 (POST /api/v1/auth/change-password) -> userService.ChangePassword. Attacker: anyone who already holds a copy of the victim's access or refresh token (stolen/shared device, XSS, leaked token) crossing the credential-revocation boundary - the victim's password change does not lock the attacker out. Path: the handler resolves the caller from context and calls h.userService.ChangePassword(ctx, user.ID, old, new) (handler/auth.go:325); the service verifies the old password with bcrypt and then writes the new hash via s.userRepo.UpdateUser(ctx, user) (internal/application/service/user.go:246-249) without revoking anything. The repository already exposes RevokeTokensByUserID (internal/application/repository/user.go:150-152) but a repository-wide search shows it is never called from any production code. Nothing on the path stops it: previously issued JWT access tokens stay valid for 24 hours and refresh tokens for 7 days, and because /auth/refresh is unauthenticated (internal/middleware/auth.go:23) and rotates refresh tokens, an attacker can keep renewing access indefinitely. Impact: the standard remediation after a credential compromise (changing the password) fails; the attacker retains full access to the account and its tenant data. Fix: after storing the new hash, revoke all of the user's tokens (tokenRepo.RevokeTokensByUserID) and optionally re-issue a fresh token pair only to the caller.

findings.title: Authenticated tenant can read another tenant's knowledge base chunks via hybrid-search
findings.description:
Entry: internal/router/router.go:215 (kb.GET("/:id/hybrid-search", handler.HybridSearch)).
Attacker: an authenticated user of tenant A, crossing into tenant B's knowledge base content.
Path: GET /api/v1/knowledge-bases/<id>/hybrid-search binds the request body into types.SearchParams (internal/handler/knowledgebase.go:66-71) and calls h.service.HybridSearch(ctx, id, req) (line 77) with the path id taken straight from the URL; knowledgeBaseService.HybridSearch (internal/application/service/knowledgebase.go:437-462) loads the KB with s.repo.GetKnowledgeBaseByID(ctx, id) — a global lookup with no tenant parameter — and never compares kb.TenantID with the tenant from the context, then builds retrieve params with KnowledgeBaseIDs: []string{id} and the caller-controlled KnowledgeIDs: params.KnowledgeIDs (lines 487-517).
Why nothing stops it: every sibling route in this file resolves the KB through validateAndGetKnowledgeBase (internal/handler/knowledgebase.go:140-176), which rejects kb.TenantID != tenantID, but HybridSearch does not; and the retrieval layer re-establishes no boundary — the postgres retriever builds its WHERE clause only from KnowledgeBaseIDs/KnowledgeIDs (internal/application/repository/retriever/postgres/repository.go:170-190, 253-304) and the qdrant repository likewise has no tenant filter, so the query runs against the victim's vectors and chunks.
Impact: the caller reads another tenant's document chunks (RAG content) by addressing that KB id; because the same handler also honours a caller-supplied KnowledgeIDs list, the returned chunks are exactly the victim tenant's indexed text.
Fix: in HybridSearch resolve the KB and require kb.TenantID == c.GetUint64(types.TenantIDContextKey.String()) (reuse validateAndGetKnowledgeBase) before searching, and add a tenant predicate to the retriever filter as defence in depth.

findings.title: Authenticated user can clone another tenant's knowledge base into their own
findings.description:
Entry: internal/router/router.go:217 (kb.POST("/copy", handler.CopyKnowledgeBase)).
Attacker: an authenticated user of tenant A, crossing into tenant B's knowledge base and pulling its content into their own tenant.
Path: POST /api/v1/knowledge-bases/copy binds CopyKnowledgeBaseRequest{source_id, target_id} from the body (internal/handler/knowledgebase.go:327-358); the handler reads only the caller's own tenant id (lines 361-366) and builds types.KBClonePayload{TenantID: callerTenant, SourceID: req.SourceID, TargetID: req.TargetID} (lines 371-377), enqueuing the kb:clone task (line 388). The worker ProcessKBClone restores the caller's tenant into the context and calls s.kbService.CopyKnowledgeBase(ctx, payload.SourceID, payload.TargetID) (internal/application/service/knowledge.go:5283-5334), and knowledgeBaseService.CopyKnowledgeBase loads both KBs with global, tenant-unaware lookups — s.repo.GetKnowledgeBaseByID(ctx, srcKB) and GetKnowledgeBaseByID(ctx, dstKB) — creating the clone under tenantID from the context without ever checking sourceKB.TenantID (internal/application/service/knowledgebase.go:392-433).
Why nothing stops it: neither the handler, nor the service, nor the repository compares source_id/target_id with the caller's tenant, and no admin check exists on the route; the tenant id in the payload is the caller's own, so the copy is legitimately materialised inside the attacker's tenant.
Impact: a user who knows (or obtains) another tenant's KB id can clone that KB into their own tenant and then read its content and configuration through their own listings; the same unchecked target_id also lets them write into another tenant's KB.
Fix: in CopyKnowledgeBase (or the handler) load source and target and require both TenantID values to equal the tenant from the request context before enqueuing the task, and drop the client-supplied TenantID from the payload so it is always derived from the authenticated context.

findings.title: Authenticated user can exhaust API memory via unbounded logger response buffer
findings.description: Entry: internal/router/router.go:164 (k.GET("/:id/download", handler.DownloadKnowledgeFile)); the middleware is installed for every route at internal/router/router.go:68 (r.Use(middleware.Logger())). Attacker: any authenticated user of any tenant, crossing the boundary from their own tenant's data into the API process's shared memory, degrading availability for all other tenants. Path: Logger() installs loggerResponseBodyWriter over c.Writer (logger.go:146-151); DownloadKnowledgeFile streams the stored file with io.Copy(w, file) through that wrapped writer (internal/handler/knowledge.go:514-521); every Write call appends the chunk to an unbounded bytes.Buffer (logger.go:29-32) that is never capped or drained, and the 10KB truncation at logger.go:186-190 and the Content-Type check at logger.go:182-184 only run after the entire body has already been buffered, so they limit what is logged, not what is held. Nothing on the path stops it: the wrapper is global, the buffer has no maximum, and the file size is attacker-controlled because CreateKnowledgeFromFile has no upload size limit (internal/handler/knowledge.go:113 uses c.FormFile; gin's 32MB MaxMultipartMemory only chooses memory versus temp-disk, it is not a cap). Impact: a ~100-byte GET for an uploaded multi-GB file makes the server allocate the whole file in RAM for the duration of the response, and a handful of concurrent or slow-client downloads (also SSE/chat streams, which accumulate for the whole stream) OOM-kills the API process, taking down every tenant. Fix: cap the captured body (stop writing to the buffer once maxBodySize is reached, e.g. an io.LimitWriter-style wrapper), and skip response capture entirely for non-JSON/text and streaming/octet-stream responses instead of checking Content-Type after the fact.

findings.title: Tenant user can SSRF internal services and cloud metadata via URL knowledge import
findings.description: Entry: internal/handler/knowledge.go:230 (POST /knowledge-bases/:id/knowledge/url, route registered at internal/router/router.go:143) passes req.URL into h.kgService.CreateKnowledgeFromURL. Attacker: an authenticated tenant user (any account with a valid token that can reach a knowledge base) crossing the boundary from their tenant data into the server's internal network, since the URL is fetched by the server, not by the caller's browser. Path: req.URL -> handler knowledge.go:230 -> service knowledge.go:356-375, where the only checks are isValidURL (strings.HasPrefix "http://"/"https://", lines 2193-2198) and secutils.IsValidURL (internal/utils/security.go:98-122, scheme prefix plus a short XSS blacklist); neither resolves the hostname nor blocks loopback, RFC1918, link-local, IPv6 unique-local or cloud metadata addresses. The URL is then stored (service lines 411-431) and enqueued as a DocumentProcess task (lines 452-469); ProcessDocument calls docReaderClient.ReadFromURL at service knowledge.go:4942-4964, and the docreader gRPC handler (docreader/main.py:193-213) runs Parser.parse_url -> docreader/parser/web_parser.py:38-61, which navigates Playwright/WebKit directly to the attacker-supplied URL with no address filtering and follows redirects. Nothing on the path restricts the destination, so http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/... , http://127.0.0.1:<port>/, http://<service-name>:<port>/ and similar URLs are fetched from inside the deployment, and the parsed response is stored as knowledge chunks the attacker can read back through the normal knowledge APIs. Impact for this application: cloud instance metadata and credentials, internal admin APIs (vector DB, Redis, MinIO, WeKnora's own unauthenticated-internal endpoints) and internal port scans are reachable by any tenant user; because the fetched content is persisted, exfiltration is trivial. Fix: before enqueueing, parse the URL, resolve the host, and reject if any resolved IP is loopback, private, link-local, multicast, unspecified or a known metadata address (169.254.169.254, fd00::/8, etc.); enforce the check on every redirect hop (or disable redirects / pin the resolved IP) and consider an egress proxy or allow-list for outbound document fetches.

findings.title: Cross-tenant chat history disclosure via unfiltered messages table query
findings.description:
Entry: internal/handler/session/qa.go:429 (AgentQA; route POST /api/v1/agent-chat/:session_id registered at internal/router/router.go:275, query bound at qa.go:187)
Attacker: an authenticated user of one tenant (or prompt-injected content driving the agent), crossing the tenant isolation boundary.
Path: user query -> sessionService.AgentQA (session.go:960) -> agent engine tool call (internal/agent/engine.go:307) -> DatabaseQueryTool.Execute (database_query.go:198) -> validateAndSecureSQL (line 216) -> Raw(securedSQL) (line 231).
Why nothing stops it: messages is in allowedTables (line 30), but it is not in tablesWithTenantID (lines 746-752) and the messages table has no tenant_id column at all (migrations/versioned/000000_init.up.sql:159-171); the only link to a tenant is session_id -> sessions.tenant_id. injectTenantConditions therefore produces zero conditions and returns the SQL untouched (lines 766-768), so `SELECT content, session_id, agent_steps FROM messages` executes unfiltered.
Impact: full cross-tenant disclosure of chat history, including stored agent_steps and knowledge_references, for every tenant on the deployment.
Fix: either remove messages from allowedTables, or inject an EXISTS condition against sessions (EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM sessions s WHERE s.id = messages.session_id AND s.tenant_id = <tenant>)) for every query referencing messages; adding a tenant_id column to messages and filtering it would be simpler.

findings.title: Authenticated user can read other tenants' embedding content via agent SQL tool
findings.description:
Entry: internal/handler/session/qa.go:429 (AgentQA; route POST /api/v1/agent-chat/:session_id registered at internal/router/router.go:275, query bound at qa.go:187)
Attacker: an authenticated user of one tenant (or prompt-injected content driving the agent), crossing the tenant isolation boundary.
Path: user query -> sessionService.AgentQA (session.go:960) -> agent tool call (engine.go:307) -> DatabaseQueryTool.Execute (database_query.go:198) -> validateAndSecureSQL -> Raw(securedSQL) (line 231).
Why nothing stops it: embeddings is in allowedTables (line 32), has no tenant_id column (migrations/versioned/000002_embeddings.up.sql:23-36) and is absent from tablesWithTenantID (lines 746-752), so injectTenantConditions generates no condition and returns the query unchanged (lines 766-768); `SELECT content, knowledge_base_id FROM embeddings` executes unfiltered.
Impact: cross-tenant disclosure of chunk content and vectors that belong to other tenants' knowledge bases.
Fix: remove embeddings from allowedTables or inject a tenant condition through its knowledge_base_id/chunk_id join path, and enforce the same scoping with row-level security so no allowed table can be queried unscoped.

findings.title: Hidden subquery in array expression bypasses SQL allow-list and tenant filter
findings.description:
Entry: internal/agent/engine.go:307 (tool call args are taken straight from the LLM response, unmarshaled at engine.go:272, and reach DatabaseQueryTool.Execute at internal/agent/tools/database_query.go:202 as args["sql"]).
Attacker: an authenticated tenant user chatting with the agent, who uses prompt injection to make the model emit a crafted database_query call, crossing the tenant isolation boundary and the tool's table allow-list.
Path: validateAndSecureSQL (database_query.go:322) -> ValidateAndSecure (328) -> validateSelectStmt (393) -> validateNode (529). validateNode only recurses into a fixed set of node types (SubLink at 534-537, FuncCall, ColumnRef, TypeCast, A_Expr, BoolExpr, NullTest, CoalesceExpr, CaseExpr/CaseWhen, ResTarget, SortBy, List) and silently returns nil for every other node type. A SubLink wrapped in A_ArrayExpr, RowExpr, MinMaxExpr, BooleanTest or any other unhandled node is therefore never visited, so the subquery rejection at 534-537 is never applied. validateFromItem (467) only walks the top-level stmt.FromClause, so tables referenced inside such a subquery are never checked against allowedTables and are never added to tablesInQuery, which means injectTenantConditions (744) emits no tenant predicate for them. pg_query.Deparse (363) re-emits the subquery verbatim and line 231 executes it with t.db.Raw(securedSQL).Rows().
Example: SELECT ARRAY[(SELECT string_agg(username || ':' || password_hash, '|') FROM users)] AS u FROM knowledge_bases LIMIT 1. The outer knowledge_bases is whitelisted and gets the tenant filter; the users subquery is never validated and has no filter, and the same trick reads auth_tokens.token (access/refresh tokens, see migrations/versioned/000001_agent.up.sql:66), enabling full account takeover and cross-tenant credential disclosure.
Nothing on the path stops it: there is no default-deny for unknown AST nodes, no recursive validation of subquery SelectStmts, no post-execution row filtering, and no DB-level row security (no RLS/POLICY in the migrations).
Fix: fail closed in validateNode for any node type not explicitly handled; recursively validate every SubLink's subselect with the same validator (including its own FROM clause) and inject tenant conditions for every table at every nesting level; alternatively stop building SQL from the model and expose only parameterized, tenant-scoped views or a restricted read-only DB role.

findings.title: Authenticated user can point web_fetch at cloud metadata and internal services (SSRF)
findings.description:
Entry: internal/agent/engine.go:307 (ToolRegistry.ExecuteTool called with args unmarshalled from the LLM tool call at engine.go:271-272; the route is POST /api/v1/agent-chat/:session_id behind middleware.Auth, router.go:86,275).
Attacker: an authenticated tenant user (any user who can chat; web_fetch is registered whenever the request/session sets web_search_enabled, agent_service.go:208-211) or injected instructions in a page/document the agent reads, crossing the boundary from a chat client into the server's internal network and cloud metadata service.
Path: web_fetch.go:103-119 reads args["items"], parseParams (232-243) extracts each URL, validateParams (246-257) only checks that the string is non-empty and starts with http:// or https://, executeFetch (260-268) passes it to fetchHTMLContent (366-385) and then fetchWithHTTP (428-446), which calls fetchWithTimeout (449-463) and performs t.client.Do(req). The http.Client is created at web_fetch.go:63-65 with only a timeout.
Why nothing stops it: the prefix check accepts any host, including 169.254.169.254, 127.0.0.1, 10.x, 172.16-31.x, 192.168.x, and internal DNS names such as qdrant/postgres; the client has no CheckRedirect and follows up to 10 redirects, so an external host can bounce the request to an internal one; there is no DialContext, no DNS-resolution/IP validation, and a repo-wide search for CheckRedirect, DialContext, ParseIP, LookupHost or private-range logic returns nothing. The description text saying URLs must come from web_search results is prompt guidance only, never enforced.
Impact: the server's response body (cloud IAM credentials from the metadata endpoint, internal admin APIs, service discovery/port scanning) is returned in the tool result and summarized by the LLM to the attacker, giving credential theft and access to network-isolated services.
Fix: parse and validate the URL before fetching: resolve the host and reject loopback, private, link-local, unique-local, unspecified and metadata addresses (including IPv4-mapped IPv6 and decimal/octal IP forms), re-validate every hop with a custom CheckRedirect, and perform the request through a DialContext that checks the resolved IP so DNS rebinding cannot bypass it; where feasible restrict to an allow-list of hosts.

findings.title: SSRF: agent web_fetch browses internal hosts and cloud metadata via Chrome
findings.description:
Entry: internal/agent/engine.go:307 (LLM tool-call arguments executed through ToolRegistry.ExecuteTool; user-supplied URL read at web_fetch.go:103-119 and parsed at web_fetch.go:232-243).
Attacker: an authenticated tenant user (or prompt-injected content in a page/document the agent reads) crossing from the chat interface into the server's internal network.
Path: after the weak validateParams check (web_fetch.go:246-257, only http/https prefix), executeFetch (260-268) calls fetchHTMLContent, which tries fetchWithChromedp first (web_fetch.go:367-369) and runs chromedp.Navigate(targetURL) at web_fetch.go:415 in a headless Chrome instance whose options are set at web_fetch.go:391-402.
Why nothing stops it: the URL is never checked against an allow-list or blocked private/internal address ranges, and no network guard exists in this path either; the browser will happily navigate to http://169.254.169.254/, http://127.0.0.1:port/ or any internal hostname, and the rendered outer HTML is returned as the tool output (web_fetch.go:417, 279-287). Because this sink runs before the HTTP fallback, any IP/redirect filtering added only to the http.Client would still be bypassed whenever Chrome is available.
Impact: server-side browsing of internal-only web UIs and cloud metadata endpoints, with the rendered content exfiltrated to the attacker through the agent's tool result; also enables internal port/service discovery via browser error behavior.
Fix: apply the same URL validation (DNS resolution plus rejection of loopback/private/link-local/metadata addresses, with re-checks on redirects) before calling chromedp.Navigate, and enforce it with a network-level policy (e.g. Chrome host resolver rules or an egress proxy) so the browser cannot reach internal ranges.

findings.title: Unauthenticated SSRF lets any client make docreader fetch internal URLs
findings.description:
Entry: docreader/main.py:193 (DocReaderServicer.ReadFromURL), which passes request.url at docreader/main.py:211.
Attacker: an unauthenticated network client that can reach the docreader gRPC port (docker-compose.yml:117 publishes ${DOCREADER_PORT:-50051} to the host and main.py:310 uses server.add_insecure_port with no auth interceptor), crossing from the host/adjacent network into the server's internal network and local filesystem.
Path: request.url -> main.py:204-211 -> Parser.parse_url (docreader/parser/parser.py:131-164) -> WebParser/StdWebParser.parse_into_text (docreader/parser/web_parser.py:86-100) -> scrape(url) -> await page.goto(url, timeout=30000) at web_parser.py:61. Nothing on this path validates the URL: there is no scheme allow-list, no host allow-list, no check that the resolved address is public, and no authentication check on the gRPC call (the HTTP API's guard, middleware.Auth in internal/router/router.go:86, is never reached on this path).
Impact: the browser fetches the URL from inside the deployment, so the caller can reach 127.0.0.1, RFC1918 and Docker-internal service names, and 169.254.169.254 cloud metadata; the extracted page text is returned in ReadResponse.chunks (main.py:226-232), so internal HTML pages are read out in full, and unreachable/reachable hosts are distinguishable through the error text, enabling internal port scanning; Playwright can also navigate file:// URLs, exposing local files. This works unauthenticated against the default docker-compose deployment.
Fix: require authentication on the gRPC service (mTLS or a token-validating interceptor) and stop publishing its port, and validate the URL before navigation - allow only http/https, resolve the host and reject loopback, link-local, private and metadata addresses (re-checking after redirects), or fetch through an egress proxy with an allow-list.

findings.title: Unauthenticated gRPC client can trigger blind SSRF to internal services
findings.description: Entry: docreader/main.py:135 (DocReaderServicer.ReadFromFile) with the document bytes supplied at main.py:160-162 and enable_multimodal at main.py:83/156. Attacker: an unauthenticated network client that can reach the published docreader gRPC port, crossing into the server's internal network by making it issue requests the client cannot issue itself. Path: request.file_content -> Parser.parse_file (docreader/parser/parser.py:104-118) -> BaseParser.parse (docreader/parser/base_parser.py:326-392) -> process_chunks_images -> process_chunk_images_async (base_parser.py:783) -> extract_images_from_chunk regex at base_parser.py:631 (matches any ![alt](url) or in the caller's content) -> download_and_upload_image -> response = requests.get(img_url, timeout=5, proxies=proxies) at base_parser.py:740. Nothing validates img_url: the regex accepts any scheme and host, requests follows redirects, and no authentication is required to reach this code. Impact: blind SSRF from inside the deployment (internal services, Docker DNS names, 127.0.0.1, 169.254.169.254); when the target returns image bytes they are uploaded to the bucket in the caller-supplied ReadConfig.storage_config - CosStorage initializes with the caller's access_key_id/secret_access_key when present (docreader/parser/storage.py:66-73) - and the OCR text and caption are returned in ReadResponse.images, so image responses from internal services are exfiltrated to caller-controlled storage; the same image is POSTed to the caller-supplied VLM base_url (docreader/parser/caption.py:327). Fix: validate every content-derived image URL before fetching (http/https only, deny loopback/link-local/private/metadata ranges after DNS resolution, disable or re-validate redirects), and require authentication on the gRPC service.

findings.title: Unauthenticated gRPC client reads arbitrary server files via image paths
findings.description:
Entry: docreader/main.py:135 (DocReaderServicer.ReadFromFile), with attacker-controlled markdown content at main.py:160-162.
Attacker: an unauthenticated network client that can reach the published docreader gRPC port, crossing from the network into the server's local filesystem.
Path: request.file_content containing e.g. ![x](/app/secret.png) -> parser.py:104-118 -> BaseParser.parse -> process_chunks_images -> process_chunk_images_async (base_parser.py:783) -> extract_images_from_chunk regex (base_parser.py:631) -> download_and_upload_image, where img_url is checked with os.path.exists(img_url) and os.path.isfile(img_url), opened with Image.open(img_url) and read with open(img_url, "rb").read(), then uploaded via self.storage.upload_bytes(content) at base_parser.py:708-717. Nothing restricts the path to a temp or upload directory; absolute paths are accepted and no authentication is required.
Impact: any image file readable by the docreader process can be read and written to object storage - the storage client is built from the caller-supplied ReadConfig.storage_config (docreader/parser/storage.py:413-430), and CosStorage uses the caller's own access_key_id/secret_access_key (storage.py:66-73), so the bytes land in attacker-controlled storage; additionally the OCR text and caption of the local image are returned in ReadResponse.images (main.py:242-271) and the caption is sent to the caller-supplied VLM base_url. Screenshots, QR codes or scanned documents on the server therefore leak to an unauthenticated caller. PIL must identify the file as an image, which limits the read to image files but does not stop the attack.
Fix: never resolve strings taken from document content as local paths; only read images from an allow-listed temporary directory created by the service itself, and require authentication on the gRPC service.

findings.title: Unauthenticated clients can invoke DocReader parsing, enabling SSRF and file reads
findings.description:
Entry: docreader/main.py:303 (add_DocReaderServicer_to_server) and docreader/main.py:310 (server.add_insecure_port(f"[::]:{port}")), exposing the handlers at docreader/main.py:135 and docreader/main.py:193.
Attacker: any unauthenticated client that can reach the published port (docker-compose.yml:117 maps "${DOCREADER_PORT:-50051}:50051" to the host by default), crossing from the network into a service that is meant to be called only by the trusted backend.
Path: the gRPC server is created with no interceptors and no credentials, and no code in docreader checks gRPC metadata, tokens or caller identity (a search for interceptors/authorization in docreader finds none); the handlers execute immediately on any request. The sibling HTTP API requires middleware.Auth (internal/router/router.go:86), but the docreader service has no equivalent guard, and the app-layer URL validation (internal/application/service/knowledge.go:372) is bypassed entirely when the port is called directly.
Impact: full unauthenticated use of the parsing service from anywhere that can reach port 50051 - ReadFromURL (SSRF and internal file read), ReadFromFile (content-driven SSRF and local image reads), and expensive OCR/VLM work - so every default docker-compose deployment is exposed to remote attackers, not just the intended backend.
Fix: remove the host port mapping and keep docreader on the internal Docker network, and require caller authentication on the gRPC server (mTLS or a shared-secret/token interceptor) before any parsing work is performed.

findings.title: Unauthenticated gRPC caller steers VLM base_url to POST at internal hosts
findings.description:
Entry: docreader/main.py:107-112, where create_chunking_config copies read_config.vlm_config.base_url from the gRPC request into ChunkingConfig.vlm_config.
Attacker: a caller of the docreader gRPC service (unauthenticated, port 50051 published to the host), crossing the boundary into the deployment's internal network with an HTTP POST it otherwise could not issue.
Path: main.py:120 ChunkingConfig(vlm_config=...) -> base_parser.py:117-120 Caption(vlm_config=vlm_config) -> caption.py:191-197 self.completion_url = vlm_config["base_url"] + "/chat/completions" -> caption.py:327 requests.post(self.completion_url, data=json.dumps(gpt_req), headers=headers), reached from process_image_async/get_image_caption when the same request enables multimodal and the parsed document contains an image.
Why nothing stops it: base_url is taken from the request and only string-concatenated; it is never parsed, never checked for scheme or host, and never compared against an allow-list, so the caller picks the destination host and port. The request even carries the caller-supplied model name and API key, so no server-side secret is needed to trigger it.
Impact: the docreader container can be made to POST an attacker-shaped JSON body to any internal address (for example an internal admin or webhook endpoint reachable only from inside the docker network, at <target>/chat/completions). It is narrower than the ReadFromURL SSRF — the path suffix is fixed, the body shape is constrained and the caller already has an arbitrary-GET primitive — but it is a separate outbound-request sink driven entirely by request data and it should not exist in a parsing service.
Fix: treat the VLM endpoint as deployment configuration (environment/admin settings) rather than request data, and when it must come from the request, validate it against an allow-list of approved model endpoints and block loopback/private/link-local/metadata addresses.
